Phased Antenna Array: an array from one EM run

An array of up to 64 × 64 elements built from the EM result of one element or a small sub-array: steered, tapered, quantised, driven or received through a circuit per element, simulated by brute force in harmonic balance when it is small, and fast enough to steer by hand.

A phased array is many copies of one antenna, each driven with its own amplitude and phase. Its pattern is the sum of the elements' patterns, and the circuit behind each element is loaded by its neighbours: the reflection a power amplifier sees changes as the beam is steered. The Phased Antenna Array component (System category, .cnl type PhasedArray) does both from one EM run — of one element, of a small sub-array, or of the whole array when it is small — so an array of thousands of elements is designed in a schematic, steered with a slider, swept, optimized and simulated in harmonic balance, with no EM run beyond the first.

The worked example is Phased Array (File ▸ New ▸ Examples): a 16 × 16 transmitter, an 8 × 8 receiver, and four power amplifiers on a 1 × 4 array, all from shipped EM results of a 5.9 GHz patch. Every number on this page comes from it.

1. Three levels of fidelity

The component reads a saved EM result (a .cemr, as an EM Field Data block does) and builds the array at one of three levels. Level left at auto picks it from the record:

Level The record Each element's pattern Coupling between elements
isolated One element The element's own, solved alone, at every position None: each element reflects its own S₁₁
embedded A sub-array (5 × 5 recommended) The sub-array's centre, edge or corner element's, by the element's position class (Patterns=classes, the default), or the centre's alone (Patterns=centre) The sub-array's, by element offset, out to the offsets it measured
exact The whole array, solved with a port per element Each port's own The record's own

The array's pattern is the sum of each element's pattern times its wave, with the element's position supplying the phase (the array factor). At exact that sum is exactly what a whole-array EM run would give. The other two are approximations, and how good they are was measured: the same patch array was solved whole at several sizes, and each level was compared with it, scanned to 0, 30, 45 and 60° in both principal planes and the diagonal, at 5.9 GHz.

Predicting From Level Worst peak realized-gain error Worst RMS pattern error (within 20 dB of the peak) Worst |ΔΓ_act| of any element
6 × 6 one element isolated 3.61 dB 4.39 dB 0.50
6 × 6 3 × 3 embedded 1.99 dB 3.32 dB 0.19
6 × 6 5 × 5 embedded, centre pattern only 1.11 dB 3.51 dB 0.095
6 × 6 5 × 5 embedded, position classes 0.75 dB 2.65 dB 0.11
1 × 16 1 × 9 embedded, position classes 0.15 dB 0.54 dB 0.027
1 × 16 one element isolated (1 × 9 shown) 2.83 dB 2.46 dB 0.45

Use a 5 × 5 sub-array. It is the smallest that sees an interior element's whole neighbourhood; a 3 × 3 does not, and an isolated element misses the coupling entirely — its active reflections are wrong by up to 0.5, which is the difference between an amplifier at its best load and one far from it. The RMS active-reflection error of the 5 × 5 is 0.04 or less at every scan. Elements farther apart than the sub-array measured are taken as uncoupled, and the run says so ("Coupling extended from the 5 × 5 sub-array: offsets to ±4 rows and ±4 columns…").

What the measurements leave out. Every record in them is a planar run, whose ground plane and laminate extend to infinity. A real board ends, and its edge diffracts; the array's lower hemisphere and the edge elements' patterns change with it. That was not measured. A record from a 3D run with a drawn, finite board carries it, at a 3D run's cost.

The pitch. dx and dy may be anything, and the array factor is exact at any pitch. But a sub-array's patterns and coupling were solved at one pitch, so at another they are wrong by an amount that grows with the difference; the run warns when the pitch differs from the record's by more than 0.02 λ (a move of 0.04 λ changed the nearest neighbours' coupling by about 0.04). An isolated record has no pitch and is never warned about.

The power balance. At embedded and isolated the radiated power and the power the elements accept are not quite consistent. PowerBalance(F1) is their ratio. On a planar record even the whole-array run's ratio is its efficiency (0.41–0.88 on these records, surface-wave loss included), so the run stays quiet within 0.1 of the centre element's own efficiency, warns beyond it, and always warns above 1, which no passive array can reach.

2. Feed mode and Elements mode

Mode Pins Use it for
feed (the default) One, F: the beamformer is inside Any size up to 64 × 64. Steering and tapering by the weights, an identical circuit per element in the channel cell, the receive side, the Phased Array tool
elements One per element, numbered row-major from the top left seen from boresight (at most 64) Small arrays driven by the circuit: an amplifier per element in harmonic balance, a hand-drawn feed network

In Feed mode the feed is split equally N ways and element n is driven through its weight Amp·e^(jφ), delayed by Delay, rounded to PhaseBits and AttenStep, and then through its own copy of the Channel cell if one is named. The split is ideal: matched, and each path isolated from the others. A taper is attenuation after an equal split, as an attenuator per channel is, so the power it takes from the edge elements is dissipated, not passed to the centre: the 16 × 16 example's −25 dB Taylor taper lowers its realized gain from the feed by 6.2 dB against uniform weights (53.90 against 60.14 dBi at boresight), for sidelobes at −24 dB instead of −12.6.

In Elements mode the weights are not used: a weight after an amplifier would rotate the load the amplifier sees, which no real phase shifter does. Steer with the sources' phases or a Phase Shifter per element. Changing Rows or Cols in Elements mode changes the pin count, so a sweep of either is refused there; adding rows keeps every existing pin where it is.

The symbol draws the aperture as seen from the front (a larger array as its top-left 8 × 8 and its size), elements switched off as hollow squares, and in Feed mode a beam tilted by θ0 with θ0 30° φ0 0° beside it when Phase is a steer().

3. Parameters

NetTerminal
11
22

The nets of an instance line, in this order. How many there are is set by Rows × Cols; the table shows Rows × Cols = 2. In Elements mode the terminals are the elements, one each, numbered row-major from the top left as seen from boresight: element n is row (n − 1) div Cols + 1, column (n − 1) mod Cols + 1. Each is over ground.

NameDefaultUnitOn schematicMeaning
Record——shownThe EM result the array is built from: a result record (.cemr) whose run kept its radiation pattern — one element, a sub-array, or the whole array.
Modefeed——elements: one pin per element, each driven by the circuit. feed: one pin, F, driving every element through the beamformer inside, each element weighted by Amp, Phase and Delay and, when Channel names one, through its own copy of the channel cell.
Rows4—shownNumber of rows, running down the aperture from the top seen from boresight. Elements mode takes at most 64 elements in all, Feed mode 4096.
Cols4—shownNumber of columns, running across the aperture from the left seen from boresight.
Latticerect——rect, or tri: every other row offset by half the column pitch.
dx25mmshownColumn pitch, a length: a number with a unit, an expression such as 0.5*lambda(f0), or a bare number in the unit beside it.
dy25mmshownRow pitch, a length, as dx.
Levelauto——How the array is formed from the record. auto takes it from the record: isolated for a one-element record, exact for a record that is this array, embedded for a sub-array of another lattice.
Patternsclasses——embedded only: classes gives each element its position class's pattern from the sub-array (corner, edge, interior); centre gives every element the centre element's.
Couplingon——on, or off: off keeps each element's own reflection and drops every coupling between elements.
Off———Elements switched off, as a list of element numbers (3,17): each is terminated in Z0 — in Elements mode inside, its pin left open; in Feed mode by its zero weight.
Amp———Feed mode: each element's amplitude, linear, evaluated once per element with n, row, col, x and y bound (taylor(-30,4), chebyshev(-30), cosq(1)). Amp[n] sets one element's. Blank is 1.
Phase—deg—Feed mode: each element's phase, degrees, evaluated per element as Amp is: steer(theta0, phi0, f0) points the beam. Phase[n] sets one element's. Blank is 0.
Delay—ns—Feed mode: each element's true time delay, evaluated per element as Amp is: steerDelay(theta0, phi0) points the beam at every frequency. Delay[n] sets one element's. Blank is 0.
PhaseBits———Feed mode: each phase is rounded to 360°/2^PhaseBits. 0 or blank is continuous.
AttenStep—dB—Feed mode: each amplitude's attenuation from the largest is rounded to this step, in dB. 0 or blank is continuous.
Channel———Feed mode: a two-port cell placed once per element between its weight and the element (its first port in, its second out), as PA1.ch[n]. Its expressions may read n, row, col, x and y. Blank connects each weight to its element directly.
Z0—Ω—Reference impedance at the elements. Blank takes the record's.
Tsky———The brightness above the horizon, kelvin: a temperature, or an expression of the elevation el (5+280*exp(-el/(5*pi/180))). The elements' noise is what their patterns see of it. Blank is the array's own temperature, the noise a passive block has.
Tground———The brightness below the horizon, kelvin, where the record's pattern reaches there (a planar record has a ground plane and does not). Blank is the array's own temperature.
RecordRows———The lattice of a record that does not store its ports' positions, its ports numbered row-major. Ignored when it does.
RecordCols———The lattice of a record that does not store its ports' positions, its ports numbered row-major. Ignored when it does.
RecordDx—mm—The lattice of a record that does not store its ports' positions, its ports numbered row-major. Ignored when it does.
RecordDy—mm—The lattice of a record that does not store its ports' positions, its ports numbered row-major. Ignored when it does.

What can be swept. Every numeric parameter is an expression, so a VAR it reads is swept by a parametric sweep, moved by a tuning slider, drawn by yield and set by the optimizer: dx, dy, Amp, Phase, Delay and their [n] overrides, PhaseBits, AttenStep, Z0, Tsky, Tground and every Rx…[k]. Rows and Cols sweep in Feed mode only. The words — Record, Mode, Level, Patterns, Lattice, Coupling, Channel — and the Off list are not swept.

Lengths. dx and dy take any length unit circuitRF knows (mm, mil, um, in…) or an expression such as 0.5*lambda(f0); a bare number takes the unit shown beside the field, as every length does.

4. Steering and tapering

Amp, Phase and Delay are evaluated once per element, with five names bound to that element:

Name Value
n Element number, 1 … N, row-major from the top left seen from boresight
row, col 1-based
x, y Position from the array's centre, in metres; columns run along x, rows down y

and five functions that read them:

Function Value
steer(theta0, phi0, f0) The phase in degrees that points a phase-shifter beam to (θ0, φ0) at f0
steerDelay(theta0, phi0) The delay in seconds that points a true-time-delay beam, at every frequency
taylor(sll, nbar) A Taylor taper of sidelobe level sll dB over the rows and the columns, 1 at the peak
chebyshev(sll) A Chebyshev taper
cosq(q) A cosine-to-the-q taper

The angles are angles: 30 deg, or a VAR whose unit column says deg. A bare number is radians, as it is to every trigonometric function, so theta0 = 30 with no unit steers to 30 radians. Write theta0 = 30 deg.

The example's transmitter, steered and tapered:

theta0 = 30 deg
phi0   = 0 deg
f0     = 5.9 GHz
PhasedArray:PA1 f Record="results/Patch 5x5.cemr" RecordRows=5 RecordCols=5 RecordDx=25.86 mm RecordDy=25.86 mm Mode=feed Rows=16 Cols=16 dx=25.86 mm dy=25.86 mm Phase=steer(theta0,phi0,f0) Amp=taylor(-25,4) PhaseBits=6 Channel=TxChannel
analysis F1 type=fields block=PA1 freq=5.9 freqUnit=GHz drive=1
analysis F2 type=fields block=PA1 freq=5.9 freqUnit=GHz drive=1
analysis SW1 type=parametric_sweep Var=theta0 Values=0,10,20,30,40,50,60 Unit=deg Inner=F2

(RecordRows…RecordDy give the sub-array's lattice; a record written since the array arrived stores its ports' positions and needs none of them.) At 30° this gives a 8.57° × 7.49° beam, a first sidelobe of −24.66 dB and 0.43 dB of scan loss. Phase[n], Amp[n] and Delay[n] set one element; Off=3,17,200 switches elements off (weight zero, terminated in Z0).

Phase shifters squint; delays do not. steer() is a phase, right at f0 only, so away from f0 the beam points elsewhere; steerDelay() points the same way at every frequency. The Phase Shifter block delays by its Phase, the opposite sign to a weight's, so a channel that steers through one writes Phase=-steer(…).

What a fields analysis on the array publishes. The pattern (farfield), as for any radiation pattern; its plane cuts, farfield.CutU, CutEtheta and CutEphi, over freq, cut (the plane's φ, degrees), angle and port; and an array group over the element axis: a, b, GammaActive, Pacc, w, wQuantised, row, col, x, y. The measurements:

Measurement Value
RealizedGainDbi(F1), GainDbi(F1), DirectivityDbi(F1) As for any pattern; realized gain is per watt available at the driven port, so it counts any gain in the channels
HpbwDeg(F1, "elevation"), HpbwDeg(F1, "azimuth") Half-power beamwidth in the two principal planes through the peak, degrees
SllDb(F1) First sidelobe level below the peak, dB
PointingErrorDeg(F1, θ, φ) The angle from (θ, φ) to the peak, both numbers of degrees. A VAR in deg reads as radians in a measure, so write PointingErrorDeg(F1, theta0*180/pi, phi0*180/pi)
ScanLossDb(F1) How much below the boresight gain the scanned peak is
GratingMarginDeg(F1) How far the nearest grating lobe is from entering visible space; negative once one has
PowerBalance(F1) Radiated over accepted power (§1)
ActiveVswrMax(F1), ActiveGamma(F1, n) The worst element's active VSWR, and element n's active reflection (complex)
BeamNfDb(F1) The noise figure from the driven port to the beam's peak

Beamwidth and sidelobes are never read off the record's grid. A 64 × 64 array's beam is 1.6° wide, so a 1° grid puts one sample across it and would read its sidelobe at −16.5 dB where it is −13.2. The cuts and these metrics are formed on a fine grid around the beam, the element pattern interpolated (it is one element's, smooth over a beamwidth) and the array factor summed exactly there. Only the overview — farfield.U, Etheta and Ephi, and the 3D view — is on the record's grid, and the run says so when that grid is coarser than a tenth of the beam.

Plot the cuts, not the overview. cuts= names the planes (degrees, comma-separated; 0,90 by default, the lattice's two principal planes). Each cut runs through boresight from −90° to +90°: a positive angle t is the direction (θ = t, φ), a negative one (θ = −t, φ + 180°), so one trace on a polar plot is the whole plane and a family over theta0 overlays on it. The step is a tenth of the array's beamwidth or finer (never finer than 0.05°, so at most 3,601 samples a plane) and the record's step divides by it, so every record direction in the plane is a sample; the run says the step it took. Pin cut and keep angle as X:

analysis F2 type=fields block=PA1 freq=5.9 freqUnit=GHz cuts=0,45,90

A sweep and the measurements. Each of these is one number per run. Under a parametric sweep they are refused with a sentence naming the cube to plot instead (F1.farfield.RealizedGainDbi over theta0, F1.array.GammaActive over theta0). The example keeps an unswept F1 for its measures and sweeps a second fields analysis, F2.

5. The channel cell

Channel=TxChannel names a cell with two pins — its first towards the beamformer, its second towards the element — and the array places one copy of it per element as PA1.ch[1], PA1.ch[2]…, an ordinary hierarchical instance. Draw it as any cell (File ▸ New Cell, a Pin for each side). Its parameters may read n, row, col, x and y too, to give one element a different channel; a channel that reads none of them is identical, which the run says, and which is what makes it fast (§9). An element switched off has its identical channel left out.

6. Receiving

A plane wave arriving at the array is RxTheta[k], RxPhi[k] (degrees), RxPd[k] (power density, dBm/m²), RxFreq[k] and RxPol[k] (theta, phi, rhcp, lhcp, or an angle from θ̂ towards φ̂). Each element receives it through its own pattern, by reciprocity, and in harmonic balance and envelope runs it is a tone, as a 1-Tone source's is, so a signal, an interferer and an LO pass through the channels together.

The array's own noise is what its patterns see. Tsky is the brightness above the horizon — a temperature, or an expression of the elevation el in radians, such as 5+280*exp(-el/0.0873) (5 K overhead, 285 K at the horizon) — and Tground below it. Left blank, both are the array's own temperature, which is the noise any passive block has. The noise is correlated between elements, and the correlation is computed from the patterns with the sky's brightness folded in.

With a fields analysis F1 driven from the receive port and an S-parameter analysis NF1 with Noise=yes:

Measurement Value
AntennaTempK(F1) The antenna temperature at the port: what the elements' noise delivers, over what a 1 K passive array would
SystemTempK(F1, NF1) Every noise referred to the elements' terminals: the antenna temperature plus the receiver's
GoverTDbK(F1, NF1) G/T, dB/K
SnrDb(F1, NF1, k, B) The SNR of incident wave k in bandwidth B (Hz)
NullDepthDb(F1, theta, phi) The receive pattern in a direction, below its peak, dB

All of them work through channels that pass signal one way only (an LNA), because they use the array's receive weights, not its transmit pattern. So does the fields analysis's own pattern on a receiving array (one given incident waves, or a Propagation Channel's Rx end): it is the receive pattern, each element's transfer to the drive port, which on a reciprocal array is the transmit pattern and behind LNAs is the beam they deliver, gain included. The example's 8 × 8 receiver at boresight: 98.6 K, 242.2 K, −2.70 dB/K and 9.02 dB in 1 MHz. Steered to 60° its G/T is −5.26 dB/K: the system temperature hardly moves, the gain does.

An interferer reaches every channel through the element's pattern, not the array's. The channels sit between the elements and the beamformer, so an interferer in a sidelobe arrives at each LNA almost at full strength, compresses and intermodulates it there, and is suppressed by the array factor only afterwards. In the example, two interferers from 30° arrive at each LNA at −73.7 dBm and at the feed at −81.7 dBm, against −44.1 dBm from boresight. That is why a phased receiver's channel linearity matters.

7. Brute force: an amplifier per element in harmonic balance

When the array is small enough to solve whole, the most direct simulation is also the most faithful: a record with a port per element, an Elements-mode array (or the EM Field Data block itself), and one power amplifier per port, all in one harmonic-balance run. Each amplifier is then loaded by its neighbours exactly as the coupling says.

analysis HB1 type=hb Tone="f0" ToneUnit=GHz MaxHarm=5
analysis SW_Pin type=parametric_sweep Var=Pin Values=-20,16,22 Inner=HB1
analysis SW_theta type=parametric_sweep Var=theta0 Values=0,15,30,45 Unit=deg Inner=SW_Pin
analysis F1 type=fields block=ARR waves=HB1

waves=HB1 forms the pattern from the harmonic-balance solution rather than from a linear solve, so each amplifier's compression shows in the beam; harmonic=k takes the k-th harmonic instead, when the record holds that frequency. A sweep around HB1 gives a pattern at every point. The array group adds Pdel, the watts delivered into each element, and TrpDbm and PeakEirpDbm are at the amplifiers' own drive: the watts radiated, and the gain times the watts delivered.

The active reflections over the loadpull contours. Plot F1.array.GammaActive on a Smith chart with element as the family and theta0 along the trace: one locus per element. Add the same trace to a plot of the amplifier's loadpull contours, and the picture says which elements leave the high-efficiency region at which angle. In the example, at 22 dBm and 45°, the two inner amplifiers' PAE falls from 68 % to 37 % while the outer two fall to 44 % and 51 %.

Under a modulated signal. waves= also takes an envelope analysis, and dirs= names up to 16 directions (peak, the time-averaged pattern's maximum, by default; theta,phi pairs in degrees, separated by ;). Each direction's radiated envelope gets the spectrum, ACLR, EVM, PAPR and CCDF the envelope analysis gives a probe; each element's active reflection is a cloud over the record; farfield.U is the time-averaged pattern and farfield.CutU its cuts. Steered to 30° at 22 dBm, the example's beam reads ACPR1 −26.3 dBc and EVM 7.6 %, and the directions off the beam −20 dBc and 19 %: the distortion leaves each element with the phase its own compression gives it, not the steering, so it does not form the beam.

8. The example's Transmit bench

The 16 × 16 array's cut in the steering plane (F2.farfield.CutU, φ = 0, at a step of 0.556° against the record's 5°) at each theta0, its realized gain at the peak against theta0 (53.90 dBi at boresight, 50.04 at 60°, counting the channels' 32 dB), and every element's active reflection at 0, 30 and 60°: the edge and corner elements differ from the interior, because their neighbours do. The worst element's active VSWR at 30° is 1.59.

9. Speed

A change of steering on a 4096-element array with a channel costs about 25 ms. Three things make that possible, and explain --analysis says which applies, in a line that starts "Fast path:" or "Full solve:":

  • No channel, or one that does not reflect: the beamformer isolates every path, so nothing returns to another element and nothing is solved; a change of weights costs the pattern sum.
  • An identical reflecting channel on a coupled array: the channel is solved once per frequency as a two-port, and the coupled array is closed with one sparse factorisation kept while only the weights change — a change of steering, taper, bits or the elements switched off is one back-substitution. Elements switched off are an update to the kept factorisation.
  • A move that reaches only the weights — a VAR read only by Amp, Phase, Delay or measurements — does not elaborate the bench again either: the last elaborated circuit is re-weighed.

What takes a bench off the fast path, each named by explain: a channel that differs per element (it reads n, row, col, x or y, and explain names the parameter that does), a nonlinear part anywhere in the circuit (an amplifier whose IP3 is not 200 counts: a linear analysis linearises it about an operating point the whole circuit sets), a complex Z0, a channel wired to a net outside itself, or a circuit wired inside the array. Off the fast path every evaluation solves the circuit as elaborated; harmonic balance of thousands of nonlinear channels is not interactive and is not presented as such.

Dragging a slider off the fast path shows the pattern with the circuit held at its last solve, labelled estimated in the Tuning panel's time readout, and solves when released (Tuning).

10. The Phased Array tool

Tools ▸ Phased Array opens on the selected array of the active schematic (or asks which). It is a view of that one instance, not a document: every edit it makes is an edit of the schematic, with undo there, so the two cannot disagree. File ▸ New ▸ Phased Array makes a cell with a Port, an 8 × 8 Feed-mode array at half a wavelength steered by steer(theta0,phi0,f0), and a fields analysis, and opens the tool on it.

Beam. The aperture as built, each element coloured by a chosen quantity: amplitude, phase, |Γ_act|, delivered power, and — from measurements named for an element, Pout3_dBm, PAE3, NF3 — the amplifier's output power and PAE or the channel's noise figure. Click an element to switch it off (it writes Off); hover for its numbers. Beside it, the realized-gain pattern in direction cosines (u, v) with the visible circle, the scan-limit circle and the grating-lobe positions, the beam marked; drag the beam to steer when the weights are a steer(), which writes theta0 and phi0 into the VAR block as one undo step on release. Below, the two principal cuts, co- and cross-polar, rectangular or polar, with the isolated array factor dimmed beneath, and the readouts: directivity, gain, realized gain, EIRP (or G/T when the bench has a GoverTDbK measurement), beamwidth in two planes, sidelobe level, pointing error, scan loss, grating-lobe margin, worst |Γ_act| and power balance. Directivity here integrates the (u, v) map, so on a coarse record it can differ from the run's own farfield.DirectivityDbi, which integrates the record's grid.

Scan maps. Realized gain and the worst element's |Γ_act| over every scan direction to the scan limit, computed in the background one steering at a time through the fast path, and started again after any edit. A scan blindness shows as a dark ring. A bench off the fast path is refused here, with the reason.

Tapers and bits. The taper family and level, the phase-shifter bits and the attenuator step; Apply writes them to Amp, PhaseBits and AttenStep.

Failures. Elements switched off at random, in memory, over many trials: the spread of gain and sidelobe level.

Frequency. Where the beam points across ±20 % of the frequency, steered by phase shifters and by true time delays.

A frame is one evaluation of the fields analysis. With the fast path it takes about 25 ms at 1024 elements and 65 ms at 4096 in a Release build.

Channel. Shown when the array is an end of a Propagation Channel. The (u, v) map draws that channel's rays of the current drop — departure directions on a transmit array, arrival directions on a receive array, each sized by its power — and the codebook's candidate beams; Beams beside it lists the ranked distinct pairs with their power through the channel, the chosen one in bold. Click a pair, or a ray on the map, to use it: the channel gets BeamSelect=index with that TxBeam/RxBeam. The check button (Apply to array) writes the selected directions into each steered array's steer() VARs and sets BeamSelect=manual. Each is one undo step. The Drop slider shows another realization of the channel and writes nothing; the scoring runs in the background, its bar beside the slider.

11. As an end of a Propagation Channel

A Propagation Channel's Tx= or Rx= names an array, and that end of the channel is the array's own elements: their patterns, their positions on the lattice, and the array's orientation (TxAz, TxEl, TxRoll, or facing the other end). The coupling is two unknowns per ray — never a matrix of receive elements by transmit elements — and each receive element takes exactly what an incident wave from that direction gives it in Receiving. Several channels may end on one receive array, and their waves add on its elements: a wanted link and an interferer, each with its own path, fading and direction of arrival.

When the array's weights are a steer(), the run picks the beam through the channel, BeamSelect=auto by default, and sets it for the run only, without elaborating again; the Channel tab above shows the candidates and lets you pick another. A Feed-mode receive array whose channel cells are identical and linear is reduced to its feed: a harmonic-balance run reports the power each channel delivers there (link:CH1:FeedPower_dBm) and, with several channels, each one's share (link:PA1:SIR_dB); an envelope run with no noise replaces the array by the reflection it presents, so a drop into 4096 elements takes seconds. With nonlinear cells, or with Noise=yes, the array is solved element by element. Every channel parameter and what the run reports: Components › Propagation Channel.

Limits

  • Rectangular and triangular lattices only (Lattice=rect or tri); no conformal or arbitrary positions.
  • 64 × 64 elements in Feed mode, 64 in Elements mode.
  • A sub-array's patterns and coupling are solved at one pitch; another pitch is warned about, not re-solved.
  • embedded truncates the coupling at the sub-array's reach, and its accuracy against a whole-array solve is the table in §1, measured on planar records with an infinite ground.
  • An incident wave at a frequency the record does not hold uses the record's nearest frequency, and says so.
  • Measurements that read the pattern are one number per run, so a parametric sweep plots their cubes instead.
